body:
Meaning and main sources

Water pollution occurs when harmful substances, disease-causing organisms or undesirable physical changes reduce the quality of water. It affects rivers, lakes, ponds, reservoirs and groundwater.

Domestic sewage, industrial discharges, agricultural runoff and improperly disposed waste are important human sources. Natural substances dissolved from rocks may also make groundwater unsafe for particular uses, including drinking.

Major categories of water contaminants

ContaminantTypical sourceMain concern
Organic wasteDomestic sewage and food-processing wasteMicrobial decomposition can reduce dissolved oxygen
Disease-causing microorganismsHuman or animal faecal contaminationWaterborne infections
Nitrates and phosphatesFertilisers and sewageExcessive algal growth
Lead, mercury and other toxic chemicalsSome industrial wastes and contaminated materialsHarmful effects on living organisms
PesticidesAgricultural runoff and seepageToxic exposure and environmental contamination
Silt and suspended solidsSoil erosion and runoffTurbidity and disturbance of aquatic habitats
Excessively heated waterSome industrial and power-generation activitiesTemperature stress on aquatic organisms

Surface-water and groundwater pollution

Rainfall flowing over agricultural fields may carry fertilisers and pesticides into streams and ponds. This is called runoff. Some dissolved substances may move downward through soil and enter groundwater through seepage or infiltration.

Groundwater contamination is not always caused by a nearby factory or farm. In some regions, naturally occurring chemicals such as arsenic or fluoride can dissolve from geological materials into groundwater. Their presence becomes a public-health concern when concentrations exceed safe drinking-water limits.

How sewage affects water quality

Sewage is wastewater carrying dissolved and suspended impurities. Domestic sewage can contain human waste, food residues, soaps, detergents, nutrients and microorganisms. When untreated sewage enters a river, decomposer microorganisms use oxygen while breaking down its organic matter. This may leave less dissolved oxygen available for fish and other aquatic organisms.

Water contaminated by human or animal faeces may contain organisms that transmit diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery. These are infectious hazards. Dissolved toxic chemicals present a different kind of hazard and may not be removed by methods intended mainly to kill microorganisms.

Potable water and the limits of appearance

Potable water is water suitable for drinking. It must be safe with respect to relevant disease-causing organisms and harmful chemical contaminants.

Water can look clear and have no unpleasant smell while still containing dissolved chemicals or infectious microorganisms. Conversely, cloudy water is not automatically proof of a particular disease-causing organism. Appearance alone cannot establish drinking-water safety.

Basic distinctions in water purification

  • Settling and filtration: Remove many suspended particles, depending on the method used. They do not necessarily remove dissolved toxic chemicals or all microorganisms.
  • Boiling: Can make water microbiologically safer by inactivating many disease-causing organisms when properly carried out. It does not reliably remove dissolved toxic metals, arsenic or fluoride.
  • Disinfection: Proper treatment with an appropriate disinfectant can control many microorganisms. The method and conditions must follow established drinking-water guidance.
  • Safe supply and treatment: Reliable drinking-water protection requires attention to both microbial contamination and relevant chemical hazards.

Protecting the source is as important as treating the water. Sewage should be managed properly, industrial effluents should not be discharged untreated, and pesticides or household chemicals should not be poured into drinking-water sources or drains.

Prelims focus

  • Sewage may contain organic waste, nutrients and disease-causing microorganisms.
  • Fertilisers and pesticides may reach water through runoff or seepage.
  • Excessively heated water can be a form of water pollution.
  • Cholera, typhoid and dysentery can spread through contaminated water.
  • Potable water means water suitable for drinking.
  • Trap: Clear-looking or boiled water is not necessarily free from dissolved toxic chemicals.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 18, Pollution of Air and Water, sections 18.6–18.9, printed pages 245–249, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 18, Wastewater Story, sections 18.1–18.6, printed pages 220–226, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 14, Natural Resources, section 14.2.1, 2018–19 edition; World Health Organization, Drinking-water, fact sheet dated 13 September 2023, sections Water and Health and Key Facts, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Water Pollution: Contaminants, Sources and Drinking-Water Safety

body:
Why excessive nutrients damage a lake

Plants and algae need nutrients for growth. Nitrogen and phosphorus are among the important nutrients required by aquatic organisms. However, when large quantities of nitrates and phosphates enter a lake or pond through sewage and agricultural runoff, they may stimulate excessive growth of algae.

This process of nutrient enrichment is associated with eutrophication. Eutrophication can occur naturally over long periods, but human activities can accelerate it substantially. Excessive algal growth is often called an algal bloom.

How algal blooms can reduce oxygen

A bloom may interfere with light reaching submerged plants. When large quantities of algae die, microorganisms break down their remains. During this decomposition, the microorganisms consume oxygen dissolved in the water.

  1. Excessive nitrogen and phosphorus enter a water body.
  2. Algae multiply rapidly under favourable conditions.
  3. Some algae and other organic matter die and begin to decompose.
  4. Decomposer microorganisms consume dissolved oxygen.
  5. Low oxygen levels may stress or kill fish and other aquatic organisms.

Dissolved oxygen and biochemical oxygen demand

Dissolved oxygen (DO) is oxygen present in water and available for aquatic organisms to use in respiration. Fish and many other aquatic animals depend on adequate dissolved oxygen.

Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) expresses the amount of oxygen required by microorganisms to break down biodegradable organic matter in water under specified conditions. At a basic level, water containing more readily decomposable organic pollution generally has a greater oxygen demand.

Therefore, heavy sewage pollution commonly produces a relationship in which BOD increases while available dissolved oxygen decreases. These are different concepts: BOD describes oxygen demand, whereas DO describes oxygen already present in water.

Biomagnification of persistent pollutants

Some pollutants can enter organisms through contaminated water or food. If a substance is persistent and is not easily broken down or eliminated, it may accumulate in living tissues.

Bioaccumulation means the buildup of a substance within an organism over time. Biomagnification means that the concentration of certain persistent substances increases at successive feeding levels of a food chain.

For example, an aquatic organism may absorb a persistent contaminant from water or food. Small fish eat many such organisms, larger fish eat smaller fish, and fish-eating birds consume the larger fish. Under suitable conditions, the concentration of the contaminant can become greater at higher trophic levels.

DDT, a persistent pesticide, and certain forms of mercury are established examples of substances associated with biomagnification. Not every pesticide, metal or water pollutant necessarily shows this behaviour.

Effects on aquatic ecosystems

Excess nutrients, low dissolved oxygen and toxic pollutants can affect aquatic life in different ways. Nutrient enrichment may trigger blooms and oxygen depletion, while toxic chemicals may directly injure organisms or move through food chains. These processes can occur together, but they should not be treated as identical.

Eutrophication: Excess nutrient enrichment and associated biological changes.
High BOD: Greater microbial oxygen demand.
Low DO: Less oxygen available to aquatic organisms.
Biomagnification: Increasing concentration of certain persistent pollutants at successive trophic levels.

Prelims focus

  • Nitrates and phosphates are major nutrients associated with eutrophication.
  • Decomposition of excessive organic matter consumes dissolved oxygen.
  • High BOD commonly indicates a greater load of biodegradable organic matter.
  • Low DO may cause fish mortality.
  • DDT and certain forms of mercury are examples of biomagnifying pollutants.
  • Trap: BOD is oxygen demand, not the quantity of oxygen already dissolved in water.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, section 16.2, Domestic Sewage and Industrial Effluents; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 18, Pollution of Air and Water, section 18.7, 2018–19 edition; United States Geological Survey, Eutrophication, sections on nutrient enrichment and algal growth, consulted 3 November 2026; United States Environmental Protection Agency, Dissolved Oxygen and Biochemical Oxygen Demand, introductory explanations, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Eutrophication, Dissolved Oxygen and Biomagnification

body:
Why healthy soil matters

Soil is more than a collection of mineral particles. It also contains air, water, decayed organic matter called humus, and living organisms such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms. Together, these components support plant growth and nutrient recycling.

Soil pollution occurs when harmful substances or other undesirable changes reduce soil quality, damage organisms or interfere with useful soil functions.

Major sources of soil contamination

  • Agricultural chemicals: Excessive or inappropriate use of pesticides, herbicides and fertilisers may harm soil organisms or contaminate nearby water.
  • Industrial waste: Improperly disposed chemicals, oils and materials containing toxic metals may contaminate soil.
  • Municipal waste: Open dumping of mixed waste can introduce harmful substances into the ground.
  • Contaminated water: Irrigation or flooding with polluted water can deposit unwanted substances in agricultural soil.
  • Leachate: Water passing through discarded waste may carry dissolved contaminants into surrounding soil or groundwater.

Effects on soil organisms and crops

Soil microorganisms help break down organic matter and recycle nutrients. Earthworms contribute to the physical condition of soil and the breakdown of organic material. Harmful chemical contamination can disturb these organisms, reduce soil fertility and impair crop growth.

Some contaminants may be absorbed by plant roots. If contaminated plants or other organisms are consumed, pollutants may enter the food chain. The amount transferred depends on the chemical and environmental conditions; the presence of a pollutant in soil does not mean that every crop will absorb it equally.

Distinguishing soil pollution from related problems

Soil erosion

Soil erosion is the removal of soil particles, especially valuable topsoil, by agents such as running water and wind. Deforestation, loss of vegetation cover and unsuitable land use can accelerate erosion. It is an important form of land degradation, but it is not the same process as chemical contamination.

Soil salinity

Soil salinity means an excessive concentration of soluble salts in soil. In poorly drained irrigated land, salts may accumulate and damage plant growth. This problem concerns the buildup of salts; it should not automatically be treated as contamination by a pesticide or industrial toxin.

Soil fertility

Soil fertility is the ability of soil to supply nutrients and suitable conditions for plant growth. A soil may lose fertility because of nutrient depletion, erosion, salinity or harmful contamination. These causes differ and therefore require different corrective approaches.

Simple prevention principles

Soil protection begins with avoiding unnecessary chemical releases. Suitable use of agricultural inputs, correct waste segregation, safe management of industrial residues and prevention of untreated wastewater discharge can reduce contamination. Maintaining vegetation cover helps protect topsoil from erosion.

Prelims focus

  • Humus and soil microorganisms contribute to soil fertility.
  • Pesticides, toxic metals and improperly disposed waste can contaminate soil.
  • Leachate is liquid that carries dissolved substances from waste.
  • Pollutants absorbed by plants may enter food chains.
  • Soil erosion removes soil particles; soil salinity involves excessive soluble salts.
  • Trap: Soil erosion, salinity and chemical pollution are related environmental concerns, but they are not identical.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 14, Natural Resources, section 14.3, Mineral Riches in the Soil, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 9, Soil, sections 9.1–9.7, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 16, Environmental Issues, sections 16.3, 16.4 and 16.8.]

pictures.alt: Soil contaminants may harm microorganisms and fertility, seep into groundwater, or enter plants through roots and possibly pass into food chains.
pictures.caption: Soil contaminants can affect plants, groundwater and food chains through different pathways.

title: Soil Pollution: Common Contaminants, Fertility and Food-Chain Effects

body:
What is chemical exposure?

Chemical exposure occurs when a substance comes into contact with the body in a way that may allow it to cause an effect. Exposure can occur at home, during agricultural activities, at workplaces or through polluted air, water and food.

The harmful effect depends on the chemical involved, its concentration, the amount and duration of exposure, the route through which it enters or contacts the body, and the susceptibility of the exposed person.

Four important exposure routes

RouteMeaningIllustrative situation
InhalationBreathing contaminated airInhaling fumes, gases, smoke or dust
IngestionSwallowing a substanceDrinking chemically contaminated water
Skin or eye contactA chemical touches exposed tissue; some substances can be absorbed through skinCleaner splashes onto skin or eyes
Entry through damaged skinA substance enters through a cut, puncture or similar injuryContamination through a wound

The route can change the type and severity of harm. For example, a corrosive cleaner may cause burns where it touches skin, while a harmful vapour may primarily affect the respiratory system when inhaled. Some substances can affect internal organs after absorption.

Hazard is different from risk

A hazard is the inherent potential of a substance or situation to cause harm. Risk concerns the likelihood and severity of harm under actual conditions of exposure.

A concentrated corrosive chemical presents a hazard because it can injure tissue. Whether a person is harmed depends on circumstances such as whether contact occurs, the amount involved and the protective measures used. A chemical can therefore remain hazardous even when careful handling keeps the risk of exposure low.

Conversely, a substance that seems familiar or is sold for household use should not be assumed harmless. An ordinary cleaning product may cause injury when misused or mixed with an incompatible chemical.

Short-term and long-term effects

An acute effect occurs after short-term exposure or develops relatively quickly, such as immediate irritation or a chemical burn. A chronic effect develops or persists over a longer period and may be associated with repeated or prolonged exposure.

Some chemicals may cause both immediate and delayed effects. Not every exposure produces disease, and different substances do not affect the body in the same way. Children and people with certain health conditions may be more susceptible to particular environmental hazards.

Reducing exposure

The most effective general approach is to prevent unnecessary contact with hazardous substances. This may involve replacing a hazardous product with a safer suitable alternative, preventing its release, improving ventilation, observing warning labels and using protective equipment where required.

Environmental-health protection therefore connects pollution control with personal safety: preventing pollutants from reaching air, water, food and soil also helps prevent human exposure.

Prelims focus

  • Inhalation is exposure through breathing.
  • Ingestion is exposure through swallowing.
  • Skin contact and entry through cuts or punctures are distinct exposure situations.
  • Hazard describes the potential for harm; risk depends on actual conditions of exposure.
  • Acute effects occur over a short period; chronic effects develop or persist over longer periods.
  • Trap: A hazardous chemical does not necessarily cause injury when there is no meaningful exposure.

[Sources: United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Chemical Hazards, section Routes of Chemical Exposure, consulted 3 November 2026; CDC/NIOSH, Skin Exposures and Effects, updated 4 March 2026, sections on skin contact and absorption; World Health Organization, Air Pollution, sections on exposure and health effects, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Chemical Exposure: Entry Routes, Hazard, Risk and Health Effects
